summary: Describes how to use Elliptic Curve Cryptography public key algorithms in the Cryptographic Message Syntax, for creating digital signatures and exchanging keys that protect content. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5753 explains how to use elliptic-curve algorithms with Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS). It specifies how to sign content and how to agree on keys that protect encrypted or authenticated messages.

subtitle: How CMS messages use elliptic-curve signatures and key agreement.

tldr.problem: CMS does not prescribe one cryptographic algorithm, so implementations need rules for using elliptic-curve algorithms consistently.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies ECDSA for SignedData and ECDH or ECMQV key agreement for protecting keys in CMS content types.
tldr.outcome: It is Informational, obsoletes RFC 3278, and defines a mandatory-to-implement baseline for supported algorithms.

facts.label: Required ECDH content suite
facts.value: SHA-256 KDF, AES-128 wrap, AES-128 CBC

today: RFC 5753 is an Informational document published in January 2010 and obsoletes RFC 3278. The unit metadata lists no RFC that later obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The CMS Elliptic-Curve Profile
sections.content:
CMS is independent of any particular cryptographic algorithm. RFC 5753 defines a profile for elliptic-curve public-key algorithms in four CMS content types: SignedData, EnvelopedData, AuthenticatedData, and AuthEnvelopedData.

SignedData uses the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA). The other types use key agreement to create a pairwise key-encryption key, which protects a content-encryption key or message-authentication key. The RFC also describes certificates used to distribute EC public keys.
sections.plainLanguage: This profile connects elliptic-curve algorithms to CMS message formats. It covers signatures and the keys used to protect message content.

sections.title: Signing CMS Content with ECDSA
sections.content:
For ECDSA signatures, SignedData uses a supported SHA digest and a matching ECDSA signature algorithm identifier. The hash named by the signature algorithm must match the digestAlgorithm field.

The signature field contains a DER-encoded ECDSA-Sig-Value, which is a sequence of the integers r and s. The receiving agent retrieves those integers and uses the CMS signature-verification process.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender signs the content using ECDSA and a supported SHA hash. The receiver reads the encoded signature values and checks the signature.

sections.title: Agreeing on Keys for Encrypted Content
sections.content:
With EnvelopedData, the sender and recipient use ephemeral-static ECDH or 1-Pass ECMQV to derive a shared secret. A key-derivation function turns that secret into a key-encryption key (KEK), which wraps the content-encryption key (CEK). The recipient uses the corresponding private key and message fields to derive the KEK and unwrap the CEK.

ECDH uses the recipient's static public key and a new ephemeral public key from the sender. ECMQV also uses the sender's static key. ECDH is specified for EnvelopedData, while ECMQV can also be used with AuthenticatedData and AuthEnvelopedData. Public keys must use uncompressed encoding support; hybrid encoding is not supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender and recipient calculate a shared key without sending that key directly. They use it to protect the key that encrypts the message content.

sections.title: Authenticated CMS Content
sections.content:
AuthenticatedData provides integrity and origin authentication without non-repudiation. AuthEnvelopedData combines authentication and encryption. Both use 1-Pass ECMQV in this profile.

For AuthenticatedData and AuthEnvelopedData, the RFC says origin authentication with ECMQV is reliable only when there is exactly one recipient. With multiple recipients, one recipient could alter content without the others noticing, so a sender concerned about this risk should create a separate message for each recipient.
sections.plainLanguage: AuthenticatedData checks message integrity, while AuthEnvelopedData also encrypts the content. The RFC warns that ECMQV origin authentication does not provide the same assurance when one message has multiple recipients.

sections.title: Required Algorithms and Curves
sections.content:
Implementations are recommended to support SignedData and EnvelopedData; AuthenticatedData and AuthEnvelopedData are optional. ECDSA with SHA-256 is mandatory for SignedData implementations. For interoperability, the RFC recommends P-192, P-224, and P-256 with SHA-256, P-384 with SHA-384, and P-521 with SHA-512.

If EnvelopedData is supported, ephemeral-static standard ECDH must be supported. The required suite uses the SHA-256 key-derivation scheme, AES-128 key wrap, and AES-128 CBC content encryption. The RFC lists additional optional combinations for ECDH, ECMQV, and authenticated content.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC sets a minimum algorithm set so separate implementations can interoperate. It also lists recommended curve and hash pairings.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC warns that cryptographic algorithms can weaken over time and that implementations depend on good random numbers. It says an elliptic-curve secret key must match the size of the group order; a larger secret key adds no security, while a smaller one can reduce it.

Processing very large keys or certificates can consume excessive resources. Implementations that use such keys before validating a certificate to a trust anchor are advised to manage cryptographic resources. The RFC recommends keeping the strength of key agreement, key derivation, key wrapping, content encryption, and curves roughly equivalent.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementations need reliable random values and algorithm choices that remain secure. They should also limit the work caused by oversized keys or certificates.
